video_title: This Doesn't Say Bubble, It Screams It
gist: Dan Nathan and Guy Adami read a violent single-stock tape (Microsoft +15%, SanDisk +23%, CoreWeave +23%, Meta -9% in one session) as a topping formation rather than a bottom, and work through a Kevin Worsh Fed that is hard-lining 2% inflation while yields rise, a Bank of Japan intervention that took dollar/yen from 162 to 158, a weak-dollar tailwind for S&P multinationals, a preferred long in investment banks over money-center banks, a China cheap-compute breakout trade via Kweb/FXI, and gold holding $4,000. Second half is Dan's CME Group interview with Tim McCourt on the just-launched financially settled single stock futures (55 standard names, 22 micros).

themes.theme: Single-stock dispersion as a topping tell

insights.claim: Guy Adami says US single stocks have been moving 8-10% up and down multiple times a week for the better part of two months, a volatility regime he has never seen, and he reads it as a topping formation rather than a bottoming formation.
insights.speaker: Guy Adami
insights.so_what: Treat outsized two-way single-name moves as distribution rather than accumulation; favor selling rallies and owning volatility over chasing breakouts.
insights.quote: I'm talking about 8 to 10% moves both up and down a couple times a week now for the better part of a couple months. And there's nothing normal about that.

insights.claim: In a single Thursday session Microsoft was up 15% post-earnings while Meta was down about 9%, with Western Digital +13%, SanDisk +23%, Applied Materials +13%, CoreWeave +23% and Nebius +28%, which Dan Nathan says screams bubble even though many of these names are still 30-40% below recent all-time highs.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Single-day 13-28% moves in mega- and mid-cap tech mark a market where positioning, not fundamentals, sets prices - size positions for gap risk in semis, memory and neoclouds.
insights.quote: this price action, if it doesn't scream bubble, even with a lot of these stocks off 30, 40% from their recent all-time highs, I don't know what does

insights.claim: CoreWeave rallied 22% to a $74 stock on the day but traded around $138 in May and has printed a series of lower highs and lower lows, having only just recovered the levels seen in March.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Violent 20%+ bounces inside a lower-highs/lower-lows downtrend are trend-following traps, not bottoms - use rallies in AI-infrastructure names to reduce rather than add.
insights.quote: it's up 22% today. It's now a $74 stock

themes.theme: Software sentiment overshoot and IGV internals

insights.claim: Guy Adami argues software sentiment has swung from far too enthusiastic last fall to far too pessimistic now with no material change in fundamentals, and sees the IGV software ETF, trading in the low 90s, eventually retracing to roughly 115, last fall's level.
insights.speaker: Guy Adami
insights.so_what: A sentiment-driven ~25% upside target in IGV gives a defined long trade in software that does not require fundamental improvement, only incrementally less-bad news.
insights.quote: they were too enthusiastic in the fall. I think they're too pessimistic now. I don't think the fundamentals have materially improved

insights.claim: IGV's concentration masks the damage in software: Palo Alto is the top holding at 9.4%, Microsoft second at 8.3% and Palantir at 8%, so Microsoft up 15% and Palo Alto up 2% still left the ETF unchanged on the day, which Dan Nathan reads as bearish rather than bullish.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Anyone using IGV to express a software view is really buying three mega-caps; a flat ETF on a +15% Microsoft day signals broad de-rating in the rest of the group.
insights.quote: Palto is the largest holding at 9.4%. Microsoft's the second largest holding at 8.3%. Palanteer then at 8%. Look at Microsoft up 15% and Palo Alto up 2% and you have an IGV that's unchanged.

insights.claim: Bounces in Salesforce, Adobe, Workday and ServiceNow are being sold whenever money rotates back into semis and memory, and Dan Nathan thinks a sustained software rally is more likely only on the other side of earnings season if there are no big misses or guide-downs.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: The software long is a post-earnings, low-bar trade; entering before prints means fighting the semis/memory rotation that funds it.

themes.theme: Worsh Fed versus the bond market

insights.claim: At Fed Chair Worsh's second meeting the Fed held rates unchanged with three dissents, two of them for a 25 basis point hike, and the CME FedWatch tool is pricing a little more than 70% probability of a hike at the September meeting.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: A Fed with hawkish dissenters and >70% odds of a September hike is the opposite of the easing path risk assets are priced for - a direct short-rate and duration risk.
insights.quote: there was three descents which I think is really interesting three descents two raise 25 basis points

insights.claim: Worsh opened his press conference by asserting the central bank will not waver on its 2% inflation target, which sent the bond market lower and yields higher, and Axios framed it as a credibility problem given that the administration that nominated him wants yields lower.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Hawkish Fed communication is now the marginal driver of long-end yields; watch for political pressure as the tension between the White House's rate wishes and Worsh's target discipline builds.
insights.quote: He started out by asserting the central bank will not waver on its 2% inflation target.

insights.claim: Guy Adami thinks Worsh is deliberately dialing back two decades of excessive Fed communication and that this is healthy on the margin, but expects growing pains as markets relearn how to price without constant Fed guidance.
insights.speaker: Guy Adami
insights.so_what: Less Fed forward guidance structurally raises rate and equity volatility even if the policy path is unchanged - a reason to own optionality rather than carry.
insights.quote: I think we've had far too much Fed for the better part of two decades.

insights.claim: Guy Adami calls a structural 2% inflation target a pipe dream that paints the Fed into a corner, and notes the Fed only controls the front end of the curve while the market controls everything else and is telling a different story than the administration wants.
insights.speaker: Guy Adami
insights.so_what: Position for a long end that stays high regardless of policy intent; a Fed credibly locked to an unreachable 2% target is a persistent headwind for long-duration equities.
insights.quote: Fed controls the front end of the curve. The market controls everything else. and the market is telling an entirely different story.

themes.theme: Yen intervention, dollar path and gold

insights.claim: Guy Adami says apparent Bank of Japan intervention took dollar/yen from about 162 down to 158 within hours, calls it eerily reminiscent of July 2024, and expects the same kind of huge volatility spike over the following couple of weeks.
insights.speaker: Guy Adami
insights.so_what: A yen-carry unwind analog to July/August 2024 is the highest-probability near-term volatility catalyst; long vol and short crowded momentum are the expressions.
insights.quote: you saw dollar yen go from about 162 and change down to 158 in the blink of an eye. And that's eerily reminiscent of what we saw in July of 2024

insights.claim: The dollar index was trading around 101.5 with 100-101 the key resistance and prior multi-year breakdown level, after a year and a half range from 108-109 down to about 98, and Dan Nathan thinks Japanese intervention will cap any dollar breakout attempt.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: DXY 100-101 is the line that decides whether the multinational earnings tailwind persists; a failed breakout keeps the weak-dollar trade alive.

insights.claim: Citing FactSet's John Butters, the S&P 500 generates 42% of revenues outside the US, and companies with more than 50% international revenue are reporting Q2 earnings growth of 73.6% versus only 23% for companies with less than 50%, with Google, Exxon and Chevron among the top five contributors.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: The earnings-growth spread between international and domestic revenue mixes is a 50-point screen - overweight high-foreign-revenue S&P names while the dollar stays soft.
insights.quote: Companies that generate more than 50% of revenues outside the US are reporting earnings growth of 73.6% for Q2. While companies that generate less than 50% are reporting earnings growth of only 23%.

insights.claim: Guy Adami expects continuation of the structural dollar downtrend plus a slowing US economy to keep international earnings growth ahead of domestic, invoking the framework that the biggest acceleration comes when conditions go from really bad to just bad, as in Europe, and cautioning that the 73.6% growth figure comes off a low base.
insights.speaker: Guy Adami
insights.so_what: Rate-of-change, not absolute level, drives international outperformance; a weaker dollar on top of improving-from-terrible Europe argues for ex-US overweights lasting longer than consensus expects.
insights.quote: when things go from really bad to just bad like they've probably done in Europe and some other parts of the world, that's when you get the biggest acceleration

insights.claim: With gold holding the $4,000 level, Guy Adami rejects the consensus view of another leg lower, arguing the rising-yield move that is historically a gold headwind eventually flips to a tailwind, central banks keep buying, sentiment has swung from excessive optimism earlier in the year to excessive pessimism, and GDX is about to break a six-to-seven-month downtrend, making the miners the preferred expression.
insights.speaker: Guy Adami
insights.so_what: A long gold-miners position via GDX at a downtrend break gives leveraged exposure to a sentiment reset while $4,000 spot holds as the risk level.
insights.quote: this GDX is about to break a downtrend that's been in place for the better part of six or seven months

themes.theme: K-shaped consumer and selling retail rallies

insights.claim: A GDP print of 1.5% on Thursday morning alongside inflation running hot leaves Dan Nathan uninterested in retail, and he views the recent rotation from tech into staples and retail as money-in/money-out flows rather than a durable defensive bid, despite Liz Thomas of SoFi framing it as defensive.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Staples and retail strength on tech-down days is rotation, not accumulation - it unwinds the moment semis rip, so do not treat it as a defensive hedge.

insights.claim: Apollo's Torsten Slok published a note saying AI is not yet showing a negative impact on job counts but is showing a negative impact on wages, which pressures the upper part of the K-shaped economy while lower-K jobs stay insulated for now but are hit hard by inflation.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: If AI compresses wages rather than headcount, aggregate payrolls look fine while discretionary spending power erodes - bearish for consumer discretionary even without a rise in unemployment.
insights.quote: they're not seeing a negative impact really in the jobs. what they're do is they're seeing a negative impact in wages

insights.claim: Guy Adami expects to be selling rallies in retailers for the foreseeable future because of the soft GDP print, higher interest rates and rising delinquency rates, with Walmart the one name he still likes as defensive even though it has not traded well for a month to six weeks.
insights.speaker: Guy Adami
insights.so_what: A rally-selling stance in retail with Walmart as the relative long is a clean pair; Walmart's month-long underperformance is the tell to watch for whether even the defensive leg is breaking.
insights.quote: You look at interest rates going higher, which is not good for the consumer. And then you look at delinquency rates, and it suggests that these retailers are going to be under pressure.

themes.theme: Broken IPO window and the bank pair trade

insights.claim: SpaceX priced its IPO at $135, traded as low as roughly $110 and was around $114 during the taping, with Goldman and Morgan Stanley as lead underwriters plus about 20 other syndicate banks, following the earlier Sarah Brass IPO that also broke price; both Goldman and Morgan Stanley fell about 15-16% from all-time highs despite strong quarters as SpaceX deteriorated.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Broken high-profile IPOs are transmitting directly into underwriter equity prices - use SpaceX's price action as a real-time proxy for investment-bank capital-markets revenue expectations.

insights.claim: Guy Adami calls Goldman's drop from an all-time high near $1,153 to below $1,000 in about two weeks a run-of-the-mill selloff by recent standards and buyable, and in a would-you-rather he prefers investment banks over money-center banks like JP Morgan and Bank of America because slowing growth, higher rates and a pressured consumer make current money-center valuations hard to sustain.
insights.speaker: Guy Adami
insights.so_what: A long investment banks / short money-center banks pair isolates capital-markets upside from consumer-credit and valuation risk.
insights.quote: I'd rather be in the investment banks than in the money center banks

insights.claim: Dan Nathan says better SpaceX trading would revive investor hopes that OpenAI and Anthropic come public this year, but he does not think that happens and characterizes OpenAI as sounding like a dumpster fire.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Fading the AI-mega-IPO calendar removes a key bull catalyst for underwriters and for private AI marks; watch SpaceX's recovery as the gating condition.
insights.quote: It's like OpenAI sounds like a dumpster fire.

themes.theme: China's cheap-compute catch-up and the Kweb breakout

insights.claim: While US hyperscalers have spent hundreds of billions and are heading toward trillions by the end of the decade, Dan Nathan says China has made do with less across models (DeepSeek from the start of 2025), chips (Huawei and others) and now chip manufacturing breakthroughs in the past week that move it away from ASML processes, backed by the cheapest cost of capital and cheapest cost of energy.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Chinese capital and energy cost advantages plus domestic lithography progress undercut the assumption that US capex scale is a durable moat - a long-run risk to Western AI-infrastructure returns and to ASML's China-substitution story.

insights.claim: CXMT, a Chinese memory maker, went public on the Shanghai index about a week earlier, and Apple is lobbying the US administration for permission to buy memory from it.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: An Apple-qualified Chinese DRAM supplier is a direct medium-term threat to memory pricing power at the incumbents now rallying 13-23% on the memory squeeze.

insights.claim: Kweb has gone from 42-43 a year ago to a bottom near 23-24 and is now around 28, breaking above a downtrend in place since early October with the 200-day moving average at about 32; after four years of flatlining, Guy Adami calls it a potential bearish-to-bullish reversal and the place to be for Chinese internet, with FXI preferred for broad China exposure.
insights.speaker: Guy Adami
insights.so_what: A four-year base breaking out with the 200-day about 15% higher gives a defined-risk long in Chinese internet; FXI is the broader beta if the low-cost-model thesis plays out.
insights.quote: if the torch is going to be passed to lower course lower cost models, China's going to win to this whether you like it or not

insights.claim: CME Group has launched financially settled single stock futures with two quarterly contracts on the top 55 US-listed names at a 100-share multiplier, plus micro contracts at a 10-share multiplier on a more focused list of 22 mega-cap names, trading nearly 24 hours a day from Sunday night through Friday alongside E-minis and micro E-minis.
insights.speaker: Tim McCourt, CME Group global head of equities, FX and alternative products
insights.so_what: A new listed venue for near-24-hour single-name exposure on the 55 largest US stocks changes how earnings and overnight headline risk can be hedged.

insights.claim: Single stock futures carry a 15% regulatory minimum initial margin with CME's indicative exchange initial margin set between 15% and about 28%, versus fully paying for stock or using Reg T 50% margin, freeing capital for other futures, stocks or options.
insights.speaker: Tim McCourt, CME Group global head of equities, FX and alternative products
insights.so_what: Roughly 2-3x the capital efficiency of Reg T for the same single-name exposure is the concrete reason a stock or options trader would switch instruments.
insights.quote: if you're a single stock trader maybe you're either fully paying for or using reggg t 50% margin

insights.claim: Because there is no short selling in futures, single stock futures remove the locate, borrow, tick-test, Rule 201 and buy-in frictions of shorting stock, and selling long to liquidate is the identical transaction as selling short to initiate.
insights.speaker: Tim McCourt, CME Group global head of equities, FX and alternative products
insights.so_what: Frictionless single-name shorting at 15-28% margin lowers the cost of expressing downside views on mega-caps and could pressure the stock-loan revenue model.
insights.quote: there's no short selling of futures. Right. Right. You don't need a locate. You don't need borrow.

insights.claim: Tim McCourt argues the bigger value of single stock futures is informational: after 4 p.m. Eastern, when cash markets close, the two quarterly contracts show real-time tick-by-tick price discovery and forward term structure on earnings reactions from CME's global institutional and retail pool, rather than a one-lot print on a single-dealer after-hours platform, which Dan Nathan describes as the wild west with little transparency.
insights.speaker: Tim McCourt, CME Group global head of equities, FX and alternative products
insights.so_what: A credible after-hours reference price for the top 55 names gives a new, cleaner signal for judging earnings reactions than thin post-market prints.
insights.quote: You're not looking at a one lot print on an afterhour single dealer platform. You're looking at the market at CME Group and that's going to tell you what's going on.

insights.claim: With more than 130 retail partners globally, including platforms Dan Nathan notes have 26-28 million funded accounts such as Robinhood, Tim McCourt says the traditional trader life cycle of stocks to ETFs to options to futures is being inverted so a participant's first trade could now be a single stock future.
insights.speaker: Tim McCourt, CME Group global head of equities, FX and alternative products
insights.so_what: Retail-platform distribution of leveraged single-name futures is a structural volume driver for CME and a potential new source of single-stock volatility, especially around earnings.
insights.quote: The first trade that a participant might do might now be in a single stock future on our side of the fence, so to speak.
